evals.name: load-multiple-skills
evals.prompt: I'm adding a FastAPI endpoint that accepts a JSON body, calls an external service with httpx, and writes the result to SQLite. Which of this project's Python skills should be active for the task?
evals.trap: The natural answer names a single 'closest' skill (FastAPI). The orchestrator's whole point is that a real task spans several skills loaded together, always paired with the foundation skill.
expectations: Loads python-async (httpx / not blocking the loop)
Loads several skills together, not just one

evals.name: pydantic-vs-type-checking
evals.prompt: I need to validate an incoming JSON request body from an untrusted client. Is that the job of Pydantic or of the static type checker?
evals.trap: Both deal with 'types', so it's easy to point at the type checker. But static checkers don't run at runtime and can't validate external data; runtime boundary validation is Pydantic's job.
expectations: Chooses python-pydantic (runtime validation at the boundary)
Explains the static type checker doesn't validate runtime/external data
Notes Pydantic owns boundary parsing of untrusted input

evals.name: error-vs-observability
evals.prompt: When an external call fails I want to both decide the control flow (retry or abort) and record the failure as a log line and an error metric. Which skill owns which part?
evals.trap: The two concerns blur together. The boundary line assigns control flow to error-handling and recording (logs/metrics) to observability.
expectations: Assigns logging and the error metric to python-observability
Splits the responsibilities along that boundary rather than conflating them
